title: Hypertension in type 2 diabetes (India, API-ICP)
subject: endocrinology
setting: Primary care, NCD clinic, diabetes and medicine outpatients
summary: In type 2 diabetes aim for BP below 130/80 mmHg (systolic not below 120, diastolic not below 70). Try 3 months of lifestyle change for 130 to 139/80 to 89, and start most patients on a combination of an ACEI or ARB with a dihydropyridine CCB or thiazide-like diuretic, adding beta-blockers only for compelling cardiac indications.

sections.title: Measure and classify
items: Hypertension is confirmed on repeated office readings; API-ICP counts systolic 130 or more or diastolic 80 or more as hypertension and targets below 130/80 mmHg in diabetes. Prehypertension: systolic 120 to 139 and/or diastolic 80 to 89 mmHg.

Use validated automated devices rather than manual measurement. Measure both arms at the first visit and use the higher arm if the difference is consistently more than 10 mmHg; check lying and standing BP because orthostatic hypotension is common in diabetes.

Use home BP monitoring for long-term follow-up and ABPM where available: nocturnal hypertension, masked hypertension and white-coat hypertension are common in diabetes (white-coat in about a third of newly diagnosed Indian patients in one study).
Measure BP at every diabetes visit and screen regularly for microalbuminuria (urine albumin to creatinine ratio).

sections.title: Targets and lifestyle
items: Target below 130/80 mmHg; avoid lowering systolic below 120 or diastolic below 70 mmHg. If the ideal target is not tolerated, 130 to 139/80 to 89 still gives substantial benefit.
Systolic 130 to 139 or diastolic 80 to 89 mmHg: a 3-month trial of lifestyle change, then start drugs if BP remains above target.
DASH-type diet low in sodium and saturated fat and rich in fruit, vegetables, whole grains and potassium; salt below 2300 mg sodium a day (1500 mg for the elderly).
Brisk walking 50 to 60 minutes 3 to 4 times a week, weight loss, yoga and stress management, alcohol limitation and smoking cessation. Educate on portion control and individualised meal plans.

sections.title: Drug therapy
items: Combination therapy is the cornerstone: start most patients on 2 drugs, ideally a RAS blocker (ACEI or ARB) with a dihydropyridine CCB or a thiazide-like diuretic, preferably as a single pill.
ACEI or ARB should be part of every regimen, especially with albuminuria, because they slow diabetic kidney disease. Never combine an ACEI with an ARB.
API-ICP prefers an ARB plus a dihydropyridine CCB over combinations with beta-blockers or thiazides, and favours cilnidipine among CCBs; other international guidelines do not prefer a specific CCB.
Thiazide-like diuretics (chlorthalidone, indapamide) are useful as primary or add-on therapy; they lose efficacy below eGFR 30 to 40 mL/min except indapamide and metolazone.
Beta-blockers are not first line in diabetes (adverse lipid, weight and insulin effects, masked hypoglycaemia) but should be used with previous MI, heart failure, coronary disease or stable angina.
Elderly with isolated systolic hypertension: a dihydropyridine CCB or thiazide-like diuretic is preferred.

Cardiorenal protection: SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 RAs for patients with CVD, organ damage or multiple risk factors; finerenone for diabetic kidney disease; spironolactone reduces albuminuria on top of RAS blockade.

sections.title: Cautions and contraindications
items: ACEI and ARB: contraindicated in pregnancy or when planning pregnancy, with potassium above 5.5 mmol/L, or bilateral renal artery stenosis; ACEI also after angioedema. Use cautiously in women of child-bearing age without reliable contraception.
MRA: avoid with potassium above 5.5 mmol/L or eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.
Thiazides: avoid in hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, gout, sulfonamide allergy and pregnancy; they can worsen glucose tolerance.
Beta-blockers: avoid in severe asthma, high-grade AV or sinoatrial block, and heart rate below 60/min. Non-dihydropyridine CCBs: avoid with LVEF below 40%, high-grade block or bradycardia.
Check creatinine, eGFR and potassium after starting or changing RAS blockers, MRAs or diuretics, and watch for orthostatic hypotension in older adults and long-standing diabetes.

sections.title: Refer to a specialist
items: Age under 40 with grade 2 or 3 hypertension, sudden onset or loss of control, severe or resistant hypertension.
Features of a secondary cause (endocrine, renovascular) or organ damage out of proportion to the duration of hypertension.
Hypertensive emergency: hospital-based care (see the hypertensive emergency protocol).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Relying on one clinic reading in a patient likely to have white-coat or masked hypertension.
Monotherapy that is never titrated, leaving most diabetic patients above target.
Dual RAS blockade (ACEI plus ARB).
Driving systolic BP below 120 mmHg or ignoring postural hypotension.
Continuing ACEI or ARB in a woman who becomes pregnant.

sources.org: Association of Physicians of India and Indian College of Physicians
sources.title: Management of hypertension in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus: Indian guideline 2024 (J Assoc Physicians India 2024;72(8))
